speaker.name: Thor Ernstsson
speaker.tagline: CEO & Founder of ArcticBlue | AI & Experimentation Leader | Entrepreneur
facts: Founder and CEO of ArcticBlue AI, which helps Fortune 500 leadership teams adopt AI through experimentation.
More than twenty years applying AI and behavioral science to human decision-making.
Has led more than 20,000 enterprise experiments; the ArcticBlue team has run over 20,000 experiments for global enterprises.
Founded Feedback Loop (from 2014), a consumer insights and rapid testing platform used by many Fortune 100 firms, acquired by DISQO.
Founded Rally Health, an AI-driven patient engagement platform acquired by UnitedHealthcare and integrated into its multi-billion-dollar digital health ecosystem.
Companies he founded have raised over $300m and exited for over $2B.
Has built products used by hundreds of millions of people.
Has worked with leadership teams across Europe, the Middle East and Australia.
Has spoken at Davos during the World Economic Forum; delivers keynotes, workshops and panels for executive audiences worldwide.

Speaking themes: building a culture of experimentation (small, measurable bets over grand transformations); leadership in AI (embodying, empowering, experimenting and expanding responsibly, taught with Duke Corporate Education).
ArcticBlue's view: more than 90% of enterprise AI initiatives fail on uncertainty, not technology; go / pivot / kill beats the 12-18 month roadmap.
speaker.voice: Direct, practitioner-to-practitioner. No hype, no filler, no invented numbers.

talks.title: Fail or Scale: The Difference Between AI Experiments and AI Pilots
alt_titles: Fail or Scale: What’s the difference between Experiments and Pilots?
talks.audience: C-suite and senior leaders who own AI budgets and roadmaps
talks.short_abstract: Most enterprise AI initiatives don’t fail on technology. They fail on uncertainty: nobody tested the assumption that mattered until a year of roadmap was spent. Thor Ernstsson, who has led more than 20,000 enterprise experiments, shows how to replace the 12-18 month pilot with small tests that end in a go, pivot or kill decision.
talks.abstract:
Pilots are built to succeed. Experiments are built to learn. That difference decides whether an AI initiative scales or quietly stalls.

Most enterprise AI initiatives fail on uncertainty, not technology: the riskiest assumption goes untested while a 12-18 month roadmap runs its course. Thor Ernstsson has led more than 20,000 enterprise experiments. In this session he shows leaders how to replace the long pilot with a run of small, fast tests, each with one hypothesis, one success signal and a go, pivot or kill decision agreed before it starts.

One example: a global insurer wanted to know whether an AI assistant would make its agents more confident selling life insurance. Instead of a rebuild, it ran one blind-reviewed test, and most reviewers chose the AI-assisted recommendation. The bigger lesson was one no strategy document would have surfaced: agents would not log into a separate tool.

Leaders leave with a way to tell a pilot from an experiment and a template for their next AI decision.
takeaways: How to tell a pilot (built to succeed) from an experiment (built to learn), and why the difference matters for AI budgets
How to write a go / pivot / kill rule before a test starts, so results turn into decisions
How to run a first AI experiment in weeks with the data and tools you already have

talks.title: Running Thousands of AI Experiments Without Breaking the Rules
alt_titles: Running Thousands of AI Experiments Without Breaking the Rules (Safely)
talks.audience: Leaders in regulated industries (healthcare, insurance, financial services): CIOs, CTOs, Chief AI Officers, risk and compliance heads
talks.short_abstract: Set your risk tolerance to zero and you can’t innovate; ignore risk and you can’t scale. Drawing on more than 20,000 enterprise experiments, Thor Ernstsson shows how regulated organizations test AI quickly and safely: sandboxes with anonymized data, clear decision rights, and governance that speeds learning up instead of shutting it down.
talks.abstract:
In regulated industries the instinct is to wait until AI is safe. Waiting is not a plan: you can always buy the technology later, but you can’t buy back the learning.

Thor Ernstsson has led more than 20,000 enterprise experiments and founded Rally Health, an AI-driven patient engagement platform acquired by UnitedHealthcare. In this session he shows how leaders in healthcare, insurance and financial services run AI experiments without putting customer data or compliance at risk.

One example: a health technology company wanted shorter support calls. Before buying anything, its legal team anonymized 200 past call transcripts. Given only about half of each call, the AI identified what the caller wanted about nine times in ten. No new system, no customer data at risk, and leadership had the evidence to invest in the real build.

Attendees learn how to set acceptable risk as a leadership decision, build a sandbox people will actually use, and give IT and risk teams a role that speeds experiments up rather than stopping them.
takeaways: Why acceptable risk is a leadership decision, and how to set it explicitly
The sandbox pattern: anonymized data and approved tools, so teams can test without touching anything real
How to split the roles: IT and risk keep it safe, leaders and champions keep it moving
sources: How We Work With AI script: health-tech call-transcript test; governance and risk tolerance
talks.notes_for_thor: Check you’re happy using the anonymized health-tech example (200 transcripts, about nine in ten) on stage.

talks.title: Turning Chaos Into Learning: AI Workslop and the Case for AI Literacy
alt_titles: Turning Chaos Into Learning: Handling AI Workslop with AI Literacy
talks.audience: Executives and the leaders of teams that already have AI tools
talks.short_abstract: Handing everyone an AI license without direction produces workslop: polished output that moves the real work onto whoever has to check it. Thor Ernstsson shows what AI literacy looks like in practice, from giving the tool a role, an outcome and limits to checking its sources, and what leaders have to model for it to spread.
talks.abstract:
Many companies have bought enterprise AI licenses and given no direction on what to do with them. The result is workslop: documents that look finished, read like a chatbot wrote them, and quietly shift the work onto the person who has to review them.

Banning the tools doesn’t fix it. Literacy does. Thor Ernstsson, founder and CEO of ArcticBlue, shares the working habits his team uses every day and teaches to executives: bring your own perspective first and send a rough draft instead of a brief; give the tool a role, an outcome and limits; ask for ten versions, not one; give it feedback instead of starting over; and check where every fact came from, because a wrong answer sounds exactly like a right one.

He also covers the leader’s part. In most organizations people are waiting for a signal that trying, and sometimes getting it wrong, is allowed. The clearest signal is a leader using AI where people can see it.
takeaways: How to spot workslop, and what it costs the people who have to review it
Five working habits that turn AI from a document generator into a teammate
What leaders need to model so AI literacy spreads beyond a few enthusiasts
history: AI Literacy keynote, Web Summit (Doha), 2026 (from Thor’s speaking materials)
sources: How We Work With AI script: licenses without direction; teammate habits; leader as the signal

talks.title: Building a Learning Organization: Lessons From 20,000+ Experiments
alt_titles: Building a Learning Organization: Results From 20k+ Experiments
How to Build a Culture of Experimentation
talks.short_abstract: AI rewards the organizations that learn fastest. Drawing on more than 20,000 enterprise experiments, Thor Ernstsson shows how to build a culture of experimentation: small, measurable bets instead of grand transformations, a standing permission to try, and champions who spread what works.
talks.abstract:
The companies getting value from AI are not the ones with the biggest budgets. They are the ones that learn fastest, and learning is a habit an organization can build.

Thor Ernstsson has spent more than twenty years applying AI and behavioral science to how people make decisions. He founded Feedback Loop, a rapid-testing platform used by many Fortune 100 firms and acquired by DISQO, and his team at ArcticBlue has run more than 20,000 experiments for global enterprises.

This session covers what separates the teams where AI sticks from the ones where it fades. In ArcticBlue’s experience it comes down to three things: people understand why it matters (mindset), know how to use it (skillset), and have tools they are allowed to use (toolset). Most companies have two of the three. Thor shows how to close the gap with a lab: protected time to try AI on real work, and a few champions who collect what works and pass it on.
takeaways: Why small, measurable bets beat grand transformation programs
How to diagnose which of mindset, skillset and toolset your organization is missing
How to set up a lab and a champion network that spreads what works
history: Culture of experimentation keynote, Front Conference
sources: facts: twenty years; Feedback Loop; 20,000+ experiments; culture-of-experimentation theme
How We Work With AI script: mindset / skillset / toolset; the lab and champions

talks.title: Leading AI Without a Playbook
talks.short_abstract: PCs, the internet and mobile took five to ten years to reach the boardroom. AI got there in about a week, and there is no playbook: not from consultants, vendors or the labs building the models. Thor Ernstsson gives executives a practical way to lead anyway: set the direction, give permission, decide the risk, and learn faster than competitors.
talks.abstract:
AI is the first technology shift every team felt at once. It can’t be delegated to IT or an innovation team, and nobody (consultants, vendors or the labs that build the models) can hand leaders a playbook that will transfer to their company.

Thor Ernstsson, founder and CEO of ArcticBlue and founder of companies acquired by UnitedHealthcare and DISQO, works with leadership teams around the world on exactly this problem. In this session he lays out what the job asks of the person at the top: embody it by using AI where people can see it, empower people with access and direction, experiment with small bets that end in decisions, and expand what works, responsibly.

He also tackles the trap many leaders are in: they tried an AI tool two years ago, it got something wrong, and they decided the technology wasn’t ready. The tool they tested no longer exists. Established companies have the data, customers and distribution to win with AI, but only if they learn faster than the newcomers.
takeaways: Why AI leadership can’t be delegated, and what only the top team can decide
A four-part leadership framework: embody, empower, experiment, expand
How to replace ‘we tried it and it wasn’t ready’ with a habit of re-testing as the tools change
